1811-1840

Caption This

Nationalism, Sectionalism, and Jacksonian Democracy

6

How this works (15–20 minutes)

  1. Look at each of the 5 images. Read the “What you’re looking at” line.
  2. Write a short, funny caption, like a meme. Pick a caption style if you want one.
  3. Then write 2–3 sentences about what is really going on. Use at least one key term from the lesson. Type the key term in English, exactly as shown.
  4. Save Progress any time. When all 5 are done, press Finished and upload the file to Canvas.

Keep it respectful: make the joke about the company, the idea, or the situation. Never joke about workers, children, immigrants, enslaved or freed people, Native peoples, anyone’s race or religion, or people who were hurt.

Image 1 of 5

A steamboat on rough water

Not done

What you’re looking at: A painting from Norton Ch. 9. A steamboat sails on rough water between two rocky cliffs. Smoke rises from its smokestack, and a large American flag flies at the back. Passengers in hats and coats stand on the deck.

  • Look at the smoke, the flag, and the rough water. How could a steamboat change travel and trade?
  • In 1824 the Supreme Court heard a case about steamboats. Who should be in charge of boats that cross state lines, a state or the federal government?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: Gibbons v. Ogden (1824)internal improvements
Image 2 of 5

A print with a ship, a loom, and a plow

Not done

What you’re looking at: A black-and-white print from Norton Ch. 9. A big sailing ship is named “John Quincy Adams of Washington.” On the left, a man works at a loom under the words “National Industry is National Wealth.” On the right, a man plows a field with two horses under the words “Agriculture is the Source of Prosperity.” Ribbons across the top say “Free Trade & Sailors’ Rights,” “No Colonial Subjection,” and “Speed the Plough.”

Heads up: This print is about a real person. Aim your joke at the slogans, the giant ship, or the way a campaign tries to promise everything at once.

  • Look at the loom, the ship, and the plow. What three parts of the economy does the print put together?
  • Henry Clay wanted a plan that helped every region. Who might like this picture? Who might say, “That is not fair to me”?

Image 3 of 5

Freedom’s Journal

Not done

What you’re looking at: A black-and-white print from Norton Ch. 9. Two portraits of men in dark coats sit above two newspaper titles. The first is “Freedom’s Journal,” dated New-York, March 14, 1828, with the line “By Jno. B. Russwurm.” The second is “The Colored American,” dated New-York, May 13, 1837. Under the first title are the words “Righteousness exalteth a nation.”

Heads up: This is a serious one. The newspaper was made by and for Black Americans at a time when most Black people were denied basic rights and many were enslaved. Write one clear, respectful line. No jokes.

  • Read the titles, the dates, and the line under the first title. What do you think this newspaper wanted its readers to know?
  • Norton says free Black men in some northern states voted for the first time, then lost that right. Why would a newspaper matter during those years?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Image 4 of 5

“King Andrew the First”

Not done

What you’re looking at: A color cartoon from Norton Ch. 10. A man with white hair wears a gold crown and a purple robe with white fur. He holds a gold scepter in one hand and a paper marked “VETO” in the other. Under his feet are torn papers marked “Constitution of the United States of America” and “Internal Improvements” and “U.S. Bank.” Norton’s title for this cartoon is “King Andrew the First.”

Heads up: This is a real person from history. Aim your joke at the crown, the robe, the scepter, or the huge VETO paper. Never joke about how he looks or about his age.

  • Look at the crown, the robe, and the VETO paper. What is the artist saying about how this president uses his power?
  • Look under his feet. What is he stepping on? Why would the artist choose those things?

Image 5 of 5

The Union Pie

Not done

What you’re looking at: A black-and-white cartoon from Norton Ch. 10. A tall pie is made of egg shapes labeled with state names. The top piece is a cracked shell labeled “S. Carolina.” At the right, a large man labeled “England” stands on a rock with a knife and fork. The title at the top is “Nullification or A Peep at South Carolina in 1832-3,” and the words at the bottom say “The Union Pie No. 1.”

Heads up: The big “England” figure is a cartoon of a country. Aim your joke at the pie, the cracked top egg, or the knife and fork. Never joke about any people or any country’s people.

  • Look at the pie. It is made of the states. What does it stand for? What happens to a pie if one piece cracks?
  • Look at the man called “England.” Why might he be hungry for this pie?
